items.title: Introduction

sections.normalized_html: A literal is a variable or a negation of a variable in a Boolean expression. For example, the following are all literals: [MATH: x, \quad y, \quad \overline{x}, \quad \overline{y}] Note that [MATH: \overline{x}] is the same as [MATH: \lnot\,x.] In contrast, the following are not literals: [MATH: \overline{\overline{x}}, \qquad x \land y, \qquad x \lor y, \qquad x \mid x]

A literal is a variable or a negation of a variable in a Boolean expression. For example, the following are all literals:
[MATH: x, \quad y, \quad \overline{x}, \quad \overline{y}]
Note that [MATH: \overline{x}] is the same as [MATH: \lnot\,x.] In contrast, the following are not literals:
[MATH: \overline{\overline{x}}, \qquad x \land y, \qquad x \lor y, \qquad x \mid x]

[MATH: x, \qquad \overline{y}, \qquad x \land y, \qquad \overline{x} \land y \land \overline{z}.]

sections.normalized_html: A formula is in disjunctive normal form (DNF) if it is a disjunction of one or more elementary conjunctions. For instance, [MATH: x, \qquad x \land y, \qquad \overline{x} \lor y, \qquad x \lor (y \land \overline{z}),\qquad (x \land y) \lor (\overline{y} \land z \land k)] are all in DNF. In contrast, the following expressions are not in DNF: [MATH: x \Rightarrow y, \qquad \overline{x \lor y}, \qquad x \lor \overline{(y \land z)}, \qquad x\lor (y \land (z\lor k))]

2. [MATH: \overline{Q} \land \overline{R}] is an elementary conjunction
3. [MATH: P \lor (Q \land R) \lor (\overline{Q} \land \overline{R} )] is a disjunctive normal form

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that a literal is a variable or a negation of a variable, and an elementary conjunction is a conjunction of one or more literals.

A formula is in disjunctive normal form (DNF) if it is a disjunction of one or more elementary conjunctions. Also [MATH: \overline{A}] means the same as [MATH: \lnot A.]

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, [MATH: P] is a variable, and [MATH: \overline{P}] is the negation of the variable. So, it's a literal.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, [MATH: \overline{Q} \land \overline{R}] is a conjunction of one or more literals.

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, [MATH: P,] [MATH: (Q \land R) ,] and [MATH: \overline{Q} \land \overline{R}] are conjunctions of one or more literals. Our formula contains a disjunction of these elementary conjunctions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

sections.normalized_html: Express [MATH: x_1 \Rightarrow (x_2 \oplus x_3)] in disjunctive normal form.
sections.readable_text: Express [MATH: x_1 \Rightarrow (x_2 \oplus x_3)] in disjunctive normal form.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In general, to write down a formula in disjunctive normal form,

  • we eliminate all instances of logical operations other than [MATH: \neg,] [MATH: \land,] [MATH: \lor,] then

  • we rewrite the expression as a disjunction of elementary conjunctions.

In this example, we proceed as follows.

  • Use the fact that [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \overline{A} \lor B] to eliminate [MATH: \Rightarrow] from the expression: [MATH: x_{1}⇒(x_{2}⊕x_{3})|≡x_{1}^(―)∨(x_{2}⊕x_{3})]

  • Use the fact that [MATH: A \oplus B \equiv (A \land \overline{B}) \lor (\overline{A} \land B)] to eliminate [MATH: \oplus] from the expression: [MATH: x_{1}^(―)∨(x_{2}⊕x_{3})≡x_{1}^(―)∨(x_{2}∧x_{3}^(―))∨(x_{2}^(―)∧x_{3})]

Notice that the final expression is a disjunction of one or more elementary conjunctions. Therefore, this is a disjunctive normal form.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A literal is a variable or a negation of a variable in a Boolean expression. For example, the following are all literals:
[MATH: x, \quad y, \quad \overline{x}, \quad \overline{y}]
Note that [MATH: \overline{x}] is the same as [MATH: \lnot\,x.] In contrast, the following are not literals:
[MATH: \overline{\overline{x}}, \qquad x \land y, \qquad x \lor y, \qquad x \mid x]

Content:
An elementary conjunction is a conjunction of one or more literals. Some examples are as follows:
[MATH: x, \qquad \overline{y}, \qquad x \land y, \qquad \overline{x} \land y \land \overline{z}.]

Content:
A formula is in disjunctive normal form (DNF) if it is a disjunction of one or more elementary conjunctions. For instance,
[MATH: x, \qquad x \land y, \qquad \overline{x} \lor y, \qquad x \lor (y \land \overline{z}),\qquad (x \land y) \lor (\overline{y} \land z \land k)]
are all in DNF.
In contrast, the following expressions are not in DNF:
[MATH: x \Rightarrow y, \qquad \overline{x \lor y}, \qquad x \lor \overline{(y \land z)}, \qquad x\lor (y \land (z\lor k))]

Content:
As we'll see, disjunctive normal formals provide a standard way of representing Boolean functions, allowing them to be compared easily.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Disjunctive Normal Forms

Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \overline{P}] is a literal
2. [MATH: \overline{Q} \land \overline{R}] is an elementary conjunction
3. [MATH: P \lor (Q \land R) \lor (\overline{Q} \land \overline{R} )] is a disjunctive normal form

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that a literal is a variable or a negation of a variable, and an elementary conjunction is a conjunction of one or more literals.

A formula is in disjunctive normal form (DNF) if it is a disjunction of one or more elementary conjunctions. Also [MATH: \overline{A}] means the same as [MATH: \lnot A.]

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, [MATH: P] is a variable, and [MATH: \overline{P}] is the negation of the variable. So, it's a literal.
- Statement II is true. Indeed, [MATH: \overline{Q} \land \overline{R}] is a conjunction of one or more literals.
- Statement III is true. Indeed, [MATH: P,] [MATH: (Q \land R) ,] and [MATH: \overline{Q} \land \overline{R}] are conjunctions of one or more literals. Our formula contains a disjunction of these elementary conjunctions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Disjunctive Normal Form of a Function

Content:
Every Boolean function can be expressed in an equivalent disjunctive normal form (DNF).
In other words, for any Boolean function [MATH: f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)], there exists an expression [MATH: D(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)] in DNF such that
[MATH: f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) \equiv D(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n).]

Content:
To write a given Boolean function in disjunctive normal form,

Content:
- we eliminate all instances of logical operations other than [MATH: \lnot, \land, \lor,] then
- we rewrite the expression as a disjunction of elementary conjunctions.

Content:
For example, let's deduce a disjunctive normal form of [MATH: x_1 \land (x_2 \Rightarrow x_3).]

Content:
- First, using the fact that [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \overline{A} \lor B,] we eliminate [MATH: \Rightarrow] from the expression:
[MATH: x_1 \land (x_2 \Rightarrow x_3) \equiv x_1 \land (\overline{x_2} \lor x_3)]
- Then, we simplify the expression by applying the laws of logic, distributing the conjunction over the disjunction:
[MATH: x_{1}∧(x_{2}^(―)∨x_{3})≡(x_{1}∧x_{2}^(―))∨(x_{1}∧x_{3})]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that
[MATH: x_1 \land (x_2 \Rightarrow x_3 ) \equiv (x_1 \land \overline{x_2}) \lor (x_1 \land x_3 ),]
where the expression on the right-hand side is in disjunctive normal form.

Content:
In this example, we used the fact that [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \overline{A} \lor B.] Some logical equivalences we might use when writing a formula in DNF are

Content:
[MATH: A⇒B|≡A^(―)∨B,; A⇔B|≡(A∧B)∨(A^(―)∧B^(―)),; A⊕B|≡(A∧B^(―))∨(A^(―)∧B).]

---

Item 6 — Example: Completing a Derivation of a Disjunctive Normal Form

Example Prompt:
Express [MATH: x_1 \Rightarrow (x_2 \oplus x_3)] in disjunctive normal form.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In general, to write down a formula in disjunctive normal form,

- we eliminate all instances of logical operations other than [MATH: \neg,] [MATH: \land,] [MATH: \lor,] then
- we rewrite the expression as a disjunction of elementary conjunctions.

In this example, we proceed as follows.

- Use the fact that [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \overline{A} \lor B] to eliminate [MATH: \Rightarrow] from the expression:
[MATH: x_{1}⇒(x_{2}⊕x_{3})|≡x_{1}^(―)∨(x_{2}⊕x_{3})]
- Use the fact that [MATH: A \oplus B \equiv (A \land \overline{B}) \lor (\overline{A} \land B)] to eliminate [MATH: \oplus] from the expression:
[MATH: x_{1}^(―)∨(x_{2}⊕x_{3})≡x_{1}^(―)∨(x_{2}∧x_{3}^(―))∨(x_{2}^(―)∧x_{3})]

Notice that the final expression is a disjunction of one or more elementary conjunctions. Therefore, this is a disjunctive normal form.

Recall the following equivalent formulas:

[MATH: A⇒B|≡A^(―)∨B; A⇔B|≡(A∧B)∨(A^(―)∧B^(―)); A⊕B|≡(A∧B^(―))∨(A^(―)∧B)]

With that in mind, let's find an equivalent disjunctive normal form to the given formula.

- Eliminate [MATH: \Rightarrow] and [MATH: \oplus] from the expression:
[MATH: x_{1}⊕(x_{2}⇒x_{3})|≡; x_{1}⊕(x_{2}^(―)∨x_{3})|≡; (x_{1}∧(x_{2}^(―)∨x_{3}^(―)))∨(x_{1}^(―)∧(x_{2}^(―)∨x_{3}))]
- Use the laws of logic to simplify the expression:
[MATH: (x_{1}∧(x_{2}^(―)∨x_{3}^(―)))∨(x_{1}^(―)∧(x_{2}^(―)∨x_{3}))|≡; (x_{1}∧(x_{2}^(―)^(―)∧x_{3}^(―)))∨(x_{1}^(―)∧(x_{2}^(―)∨x_{3}))|≡; (x_{1}∧x_{2}∧x_{3}^(―))∨(x_{1}^(―)∧(x_{2}^(―)∨x_{3}))|≡; (x_{1}∧x 2∧x_{3}^(―))∨(x 1 ―∧x_{2}^(―))∨(x 1 ―∧x_{3})]

The final expression is in disjunctive normal form.
